utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us first cover a few more documents, Mr. Milanovic. I have here in front of me tab 153, Exhibit 352. It relates again to a letter to the Chief of Staff of the General Staff. Please look at it. Let me draw your attention to the document. The request is for some rockets and ammunition. Look, it says, Republic of Serbian Krajina, Ministry of Defence, Knin, 8th of April, 1993. And in the right-hand corner at the bottom, with the incoming stamp, it says received on the 7th of April, 1993. Don't you think, Mr. Milanovic, that this is a forgery? How can a document be received a day prior to the date when it was sent? Somebody was very careless when drafting this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note that the dates do not agree, but I guarantee that the stamp and the signature are authentic, because I know Mr. Dusko Babic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no observation to make regarding this discrepancy in dates?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then there's a letter that I have taken out of a tab, 00525574. The Serbian National Council is addressing a letter to the Presidency of the SFRY on the 28th of May, 1991. It was signed by Ilija Petrovic, as it is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit 327, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to comment on this with regard to the contents of this letter. Let me tell you in advance before I quote parts of it that I would like you to say whether what is stated in the letter was your position at the time in the area. Was it correct? Was it based on facts and addressed to the Presidency of the SFRY and received by the Presidency of the SFRY on the 30th of February [sic], as it is stated here, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then it says: "Confronted with the unwillingness of the Presidency of the SFRY and the Federal Executive Council to assume their constitutional responsibilities to permanently remove inter-ethnic conflicts in the present-day Republic of Croatia, to prevent armed conflict and establish disputed questions due to which inter-ethnic problems arise, and to ensure a democratic dialogue for their resolution." And then it says: "The Serbian National Council in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem warns the SFRY presidency and the Federal Executive Council that inter-ethnic conflicts in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem are getting more intensified regardless of the presence of the federal SUP and the Yugoslav People's Army and of their obligations assumed by sending them to the area." Then it says: "It has already become customary under darkness various explosive devices to be activated at the entry to Serbian villages and to fire at Serb houses and mistreat unarmed Serb inhabitants, for Serb workers to be fired, for economic and other property owned by Serbs to be demolished, for medical facilities to not provide appropriate treatment to ethnic Serbs, for armed citizens, members of Croatia's so-called political parties, intercept adults and children and submit them to terror of the 'young Croatian democracy.'" Tell me, are these all events that occurred at the time as is stated in this letter addressed to the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the federal government? Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the things listed in this letter, parts are true, and I am aware of them, and some parts I cannot say because I didn't personally see it nor feel the consequences. For example, in the area in which I lived, in the month of February 1991 there was no firing at houses, et cetera, but Serbs were fired in some institutions in which they were employed. I never heard of hospitals refusing to extend medical aid, for instance. And I heard of some other excesses but not of others that are listed here in the month of February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear about all the excesses referred to in this letter, or were some of them fabricated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These excesses, in my judgement, occurred from May up until August 1991, when armed conflict started in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I never heard of children being terrorised in February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear of children being terrorised?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never specifically did I hear children being terrorised unless the implication is to the time of war when everyone was terrorised and the children in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the activities of Tomislav Mercep and his groups for silent liquidations and murdering of women and children in the area at any time at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of conflicts, I frequently -- or, rather, I never entered the Vukovar and the area in which Mercep moved about, but I did hear from several information media and individuals that this did occur in the city of Vukovar and its environs, and it was perpetrated by Mercep and his groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of children being killed, civilians being killed? Did you have occasion to learn anything about such events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the beginning of the war, I did hear that civilians were killed, civilians in Vukovar, and there was a story about children, but it was never confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency is criticised in this letter, saying that: "The programme of measures and activities for a lasting settlement of inter-ethnic conflicts adopted by the Presidency on the 9th of May is a trick for the Serbs; public law and order and safety are guaranteed in accordance with the constitutional legal system of the Republic of Croatia. In conditions when the Republic of Croatia does not recognise the legal system of the Federation, the Serbs who live in the area are left defenseless in the face of Croatian state terror." And then it says: "Although the Presidency recommends that only legal local organs of internal affairs should move in the crisis areas, it is indirectly allowing the free movement of armed formations and armed citizens who, in accordance with the Croatian legal system, have been turned into legal local police organs. Since the Serbs are the only ones without arms and do not have their own armed units, it follows that the Presidency has, by its decision, actually given agreement to Croatian state terror to launch an open hunt against Serbs. All police stations in Croatia have classified lists of Serbs who allegedly participated in an armed rebellion and who need to be arrested or deprived of their lives, killed." And then there is reference to an example of the arrest of a judge in Vukovar, et cetera. Are you familiar with these events?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am with some, but for instance, I do not remember that there were lists in February 1991 of people charged with armed rebellion, because an armed rebellion had still not occurred in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. We're talking about February 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to read when it was received in the Presidency. It's not February. It's in May. I apologise. We're referring to the month of May, not February.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then that is quite possible. I also note the error now, as this was received by fax. It says the 29th of May, 1991, in the top left-hand corner. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And it's dated the 28th of May and sent the following day. Now that we have corrected or at least clarified the question of the date, did all these things happen at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible now that Croats had such lists, as this was after Borovo Selo. So it's quite possible that Croats did have lists of persons who took part in the armed conflict in Borovo Selo - let us call it that - and that they asked that they be taken into custody. However, there was always a problem with regard to whether Croatia was entitled to expand its police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not enter into that now. I'm asking you about things that you can testify about. I'm asking you about what is written in this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can answer. He can't just answer yes to your questions. You must give him the opportunity to answer. He said there was a problem with regard to whether Croatia was entitled to expand its police forces. Now, if you want to comment, Mr. Milanovic, about this letter, you're free to do so on what the accused is asking you, and don't let him interrupt you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, please comment. Continue with your observations if you feel I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I didn't interrupt you. Then it goes on to say: "Though the Serbian people have agreed to the formation of a parity group for negotiations and selected the negotiators, it is obvious that the Presidency and the Presidencies of Yugoslavia did not expect an armed force to accept negotiations with unarmed Serbs. The decision of the Presidency of the 9th of May, 1991, is an entry ticket to a kind of new Jasenovac for the Serb people." That is what is written in this letter of the National Council. Did you share that view in those days, that is in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, but I did think that major problems would occur, because I followed the work of the Presidency of Yugoslavia which appeared to be -- did not function smoothly, and I think that the presidents of the republics had already started to organise those well-known meetings. None of it proved fruitful, and it couldn't be called a peaceful settlement. And already by then, that is the 9th of May, we had the events in Borovo Selo, and both peoples started to arm themselves, and one could feel the war in the offing. And the international community had still not sent its representatives to the area so that the conditions were there for the war to break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this letter of the Serbian National Council, there is reference to unarmed Serbs. Were the Serbs at the time armed or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, on the 9th of May, 1991, or the 28th of May, 1991, both peoples had started to arm themselves, first with sidearms and sports weapons and later on with other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why in the last paragraph it says: "Because of all this and to avoid the threat to the survival of the Serb national being, the Serb people from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem will be forced to self-organise themselves and to prepare for self-defence." And then it goes on to say: "To avoid any possible military conflict, the Serb National Council is the only legitimate organ. Demands from the Federal Executive Council and the Presidency within the deadline they defined themselves of the next ten days to fulfil the obligation that Yugoslavia expects from them," because they had set a deadline for the disarming of those formations and for restoring some sort of order. Do you remember that? Is that right, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with this last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And with the other statements of the Serbian National Council above, that you don't agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I partially agree and partially disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Look, please, at the documents that were tendered here en masse. Tell me, please, what does this one show? For instance, documents have been produced. I assume some sort of financial documents, accounts and bills of Zastava Promet Sombor, 02290394, ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are these the ones which were produced through the witness? Exhibit 549, is it? Is it one of the tabs, Mr. Milosevic? Just a moment. Is it tab 18?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 18, Your Honour yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 18.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have tab indication here, Mr. May, but whatever I have I received from the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 02290394. It's a bill from Zastava Promet in Sombor for T-shirts; belts; handcuffs; belt cases; berets, three. And then under the next number, this one ends with 394, then 395 again a copy of the same bill for 30 T-shirts, et cetera. Again three berets, cases, et cetera. These were purchased by the training centre of the TO. It says the purchaser is the special training centre for the Territorial Defence of the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem Erdut, purchased in Sombor. Then we have this bill as one document, then the same document -- same bill as another document. So tell me, please, what -- I don't know how to put it. In producing these documents, what is the point? The fact that they purchased these things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to say. That's for the Prosecution to say, whether there's any point. All the witness can do is comment on the document if you have any question you want to ask him about it. Whether there is any point to it we'll have to decide. It will be a matter for us to decide whether there is any significance in this at all. Do you want to ask him anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as you can see, this is produced on two pieces of paper, the same copy of a totally insignificant bill, and I am just drawing your attention that we are being flooded with piles and piles of valueless documents. There's a third, 02290396. Again Zastava Promet Sombor. Against -- again there is reference to "termo dukx", again the training centre in Sombor. And then on the next document bearing the following number, again 0397, I assume the witness, since these exhibits are being tendered through him, has some sort of criteria on the basis of which he considers these exhibits significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's really not for him to say whether the exhibits are significant. He can comment on them, of course, if he knows anything about them, but it's for the Prosecution to say whether there's any significance in them or not. Let's ask. Mr. Milanovic, you see these various invoices. Did you come across invoices like this when you were working as the assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as these invoices are concerned, all I can say is that they are correct. I see the date, that the date is the 27th of November, in fact -- or the 7th of November, 1991, and the authorities have still not started functioning properly. I'm not sure that all the ministries had actually been established at the time. I wasn't working in the Defence Ministry at the time, but I do have some information about it and know that during that period of time, various units in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem did receive their supplies from any source they could, especially from the work organisations and companies that were close by. So they were given assistance by them, and they were able to procure equipment and various goods through them, and they would send in their bills, their invoices to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the work organisations, such as this centre for special training, for example, at the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It sent this invoice to the work organisation DP Dalj from Dalj. That's all I can say on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, that means that the training centre went to a shop in Sombor and bought these T-shirts, berets, and whatever. That's how it came by the necessary equipment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just hurry up, because my time is going to run out soon. Would you take a look at the list by the owner of the account in the Sombor branch, for example. And that's on page 0087699. And then the next one or two pages that follow after that, they are the account owners or invoice owners, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the number of that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 20, Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They're all the accounts, different ones of private entrepreneurs, the proprietors of various coffee bars, and so on and so forth, shops, retail establishments, agricultural farms, factory farms, and so on. There are a lot of factory farms here. The employment bureau, the health fund, the various local communities, villages, and so on, primary schools, cinema club, bowling club, a butcher's shop, and so on. So these were all people who had opened accounts, companies opening accounts or local communities opening their various accounts for them to do business. And this was registered by the social accounting service, the Sombor branch, and they opened their accounts in the nearest branches, in the Sombor branch for them to be able to undertake business transactions. Isn't that correct, Mr. Milanovic? So what has this to do with anything? Take a look at all those lists. There are several hundred different account holders, both individuals and companies, private individuals and legal entities. And even we see the Red Cross and the youth travel association, right up to the bowling clubs and all the rest. So what's special in all this about them opening these accounts for them to be able to function normally and engage in business? This is elemental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put the question this way: Do these -- do these documents show, Mr. Milanovic, do you agree with the accused, that they simply show that these businesses were functioning normally, that these organisations were functioning normally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document proves the following: We're dealing with the 23rd of January, 1992. The balance and payments and payments transactions with Croatia was completely cut off and that all work organisations from the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem opened their own new accounts at the social accounting service in the Republic of Serbia for the Sombor and Odzak regions. And I'm sure there were some other towns as well, for them to be able to engage in business. They were not able to trade before that because the payments transactions with Croatia had been cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who cut off the payments transactions? Did they do that or did the social accounting service of Croatia quite simply cease to make any payments to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the war had started, it was physically impossible to have any contacts, and I don't believe that either side ceased to cooperate. It was the war that put a stop to all transactions, including this kind of transaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's no purpose in me going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milanovic, I remember that you told us that among the account owners in this list is included the budget of Serbian district of Slavonia, Srem, Baranja, and Western Srem in the name of Goran Hadzic. Am I correct? If you look at the second page in B/C/S probably, under the number of 630-70008.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 630-70008 you said. What I remember is this: There was a decision to open up this account because the government of the region had some expenditure for its functioning, travelling expenses, its ministers and politicians, those who delved in politics and assumed positions at the time, and that is why this particular account was opened. But the signatory of that account was Goran Hadzic, who was at the same time the prime minister of the Serb district. So he was the signatory of the account, which means he could be the -- have been the beneficiary, but so could the other government members as well. They could have been beneficiaries too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as this name is concerned, Mr. Milanovic, he comes under the column of persons representing firms or company representatives, because it states the account number, the name, the location, and the company representatives. Those are the columns in these lists. And just as the veterinary station of Beli Manastir is represented probably by its director, the budget similarly is represented -- the budget of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem is represented or the funds can be signed by the president of that district, and he is the individual who is the authorised person to represent it and has a registered signature to represent that organisation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The practice in work organisations, in companies, and in political bodies and organs of a state is usually that people dealing with finance are those individuals, whether they were people who were head of the financial department or some other department, but having to do with monies. And if the decision was taken for the authorised person to be Goran Hadzic, this is not at issue, but it would be more logical had it been the Finance Minister, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean more logical? What does "more logical" mean? Do you consider that this was an extraordinary situation, that it was unusual for Goran Hadzic to represent the budget of the district and to say how the funds were to be used that were on the account? Was that out of the ordinary in any way then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "more logical", I consider that the prime minister has enough duties elsewhere which are significant for the state, whereas the Minister of Finance would necessarily deal with financial matters. It comes under his sector, which means that he has to sign invoices and accounts daily, keep records of this kind and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There's no -- really no purpose in going on with this any further, because matters seem to be quite clear when we look at these, this mass of financial data and these lists. A moment ago, I received a correction of an intercept, a corrigendum to an intercept. I think there was a printing or typing error somewhere, and it relates to CD 1/28/08-01-212 of the 30th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's tab 10 of the intercept binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first thing that was corrected is this: It says -- I have it in English. "Well, I took this paper so that Vladan and Ratko could have a look at it. [In English] The declaration itself is good. I've read it." [Interpretation] The question asked was who this was about, because the names used are Vladan and Ratko. And we're dealing with some legal documents here, a declaration, in actual fact, constitutional matter, things of that type. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, then my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Ratko Markovic, I assume that's not at issue. He is Professor of law, Professor Dr. Ratko Markovic is his name and title? And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vladan was Professor Dr. Vladan Kutlesic, and both those two men were participants in the writing of the constitution of Serbia and Yugoslavia, which means they were prominent legal men who looked at documents; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is asked is their professional opinion with respect to some legal documents that had a legal and constitutional nature. Isn't that right, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, and I assume correctly, because it says Vladan and Ratko here, and as I said that I did some work with respect to legal issues with Mr. Ratko Markovic, then I assume correctly that that was the people that were referred to, and I recognise this in the conversation mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what they're talking about is how relations were being set up and discussion between two legal men with respect to the declaration and the relations asserted therein or treated in any other way. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And as far as I understand it or as far as I remember it, I haven't read it now, you are recommending them to your -- you tell your interlocutors to have a look at the subject matter from a professional viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. There are very many intercepts here. When did you listen to all these conversations for you to be able to identify them shown to you by the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but it was approximately three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to identify some of them on the basis of the people you knew and the rest on the basis of the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More on the basis of the people that I knew and a fewer number that I knew through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I think this is tab 8 that I want to look at next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 0206699. As what is being quoted here, I think this is the substance of it. What is stated is the following: "Slobodan Milosevic, SM," and we're talking about this intercepted conversation, Radovan Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date, Mr. Milosevic, so we can identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 25th of December, 1991. It is tab 8, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I say to Karadzic: "... the Presidency, and you are making certain mistakes. You have forgotten to see the most important thing when you question Alija Izetbegovic." Radovan Karadzic and myself. Then I say: "The worst thing isn't that he is doing it without the consensus of all three peoples but ..." And then Karadzic says: "But he is doing a criminal act." And I go back to what I was saying: "The worst thing is the following: That Bosnia-Herzegovina, by a decision of this kind, has violated its own constitution." And Karadzic says: "Yes, we've already said that." And then Milosevic again: "The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina defines Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republic within the frameworks of Yugoslavia. So it's different to the constitution of Macedonia, Croatia and Slovenia," 'it' meaning the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "They at least issued their own constitutions defining themselves as independent states." And then Karadzic says: "Yes, yes." Then once again I go on to explain and say that he hasn't only violated the constitution in the sense that you need the consensus of all three peoples, he's also -- he's also changed the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina without changing its constitution, because it is in the constitution of the BH that it is stated that it is a Yugoslav republic, a Republic of Yugoslavia. And then we go on to say that it is necessary to clear matters up in a calm, logical, and legal procedure. Is that then the best proof that efforts were being made legally and lawfully, in a constitutional manner, to set up the relationships here and that nobody spoke of any war here or violence of any kind but quite the contrary, the need to respect the constitution and for those relationships to be set up accordingly, if necessary through changes and amendments, but pursuant to the procedure, the constitution of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on and so forth. And as you yourself looked at these intercepted conversations, that would be the essence of them. Isn't that right, Mr. Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did listen to this conversation, and it is an authentic one. And among other things in this conversation, you said that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Milanovic. I won't pursue this line of questioning, but the endeavours, I suppose, are clear. I have to ask some more questions to clarify certain matters. During your examination-in-chief here, you spoke about the presence of Kosutic, Crncevic, Cvijan, or rather, you were asked about the Assembly and their presence at the Assembly. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These people were mentioned, and they attended the Assembly as guests, in the capacity of guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to establish. You call -- invited people from Belgrade to be guests. They had no active role to play. They had merely come having been invited as guests, they took their seats in the front row and listened to your Assembly meeting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were present as guests attending the district's Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any active role to play in the work of the Assembly or were they just there in the capacity of guests being -- having been invited by you to attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were merely guests. They were not active participants at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As is customary. When a guest comes in, he sits down, listens to what's going on, and then he goes home and that's all; is that right? Now, tell me this, please: You said during the examination-in-chief, or in response to a question put to you by the opposite side, that the Croats from your village left at the end of June 1991, when the war operations began; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you discussed the safety of the Croats at a meeting with them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did they ask of you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask for anything in particular. We had a meeting as to what should be done next, and they asked me at the meeting whether we could guarantee their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that we couldn't guarantee their safety and that they should decide themselves at their own risk whether they would stay in the village or leave, and when the situation calms down, they could come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why couldn't you guarantee their safety?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the environs, there were active operations ongoing already, and we didn't know who would come, who wouldn't come, what would happen. We sought to save ourselves, and we thought that we wouldn't be able to care for them, and that is when they decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming that they decided to leave out of fear for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have one minute more. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't watching the time. I wanted to ask the witness something about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict, you lived in a poor family, you engaged in the production of melons, watermelons, you drove an asphalt-making machine in the company for roads?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever lived in a poor family, because the rule in the last 50 years or, rather, my family was thought to be the wealthiest in that village in the last 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a company called Famis, in the name of your wife?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About two years ago, we have a company that is called Famis, and it is in my wife's name, and she's working together with the other family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you have two apartments in Belgrade and a villa at Dedinje or Senjak?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that I have two apartments. I have one apartment in Dedinje and a small house of 106 square metres in Senjak. If that can be considered a villa, then I accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many cars do you own?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant to see how someone who was a tradesman in watermelon became a very rich man in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can't see any relevance in that at all even if true. He's told you he was not simply a tradesman in watermelons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have occasion to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Milanovic, were you, in connection with your testimony, a suspect at any point in time or were you asked to testify only as a witness, and how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm 48 years old and never in my life was I suspected of anything. And this applies to the present as well. And in a conversation with an investigator, Vladimir Dzuro, I agreed to come to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you get in touch with Vladimir Dzuro and how did the idea come about for you to testify?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but if I could think it over closely, I would remember the name. Anyway, someone gave him my telephone number. He called me up and came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was no mention of any possible grounds for you to be suspected for certain things from the period about which you're testifying now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that I cannot be suspected, because I know what I did, and especially as I wasn't active until the end of 1991, that is the beginning of 1992 when active combat started. So there's absolutely no grounds for suspecting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have had well over your time, Mr. Milosevic. I'm going to ask Mr. Kay if he has any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just looking at paragraph 2 of your statement, and it seems that in 1990, you were president of your local commune and were not involved in politics in any serious way. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was the president of the local commune for several years, perhaps the youngest one in the former Yugoslavia, and I was involved in politics from my early youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you been active in a -- in a political party, then, before 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the only one; that is, I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After May 1990 and the elections in Croatia, it was then that you became involved in the political party in Croatia which represented the interest of the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was not a member of the party representing the interests of the Serbs, but I joined the authorities as president of the local commune, and until the very end, I didn't join a single party, and I am not a member of any party today, and not of the SDS either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you were on the Serbian National Council, would it be right to describe you as an independent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were appointed the acting Minister of Defence within the Serbian Krajina as an independent, without representing any political party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you remained in that position, working with various of the leaders of the time, Goran Hadzic, Milan Babic, Milan Martic? You were working with those people on the Serbian National Council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian National Council very little, but in the government of Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the three men I just mentioned there, Milan Martic, Goran Hadzic, Milan Babic, it's quite clear from your statement, and I'm looking at paragraph 39 here, that there was a -- a power struggle between those three. I'm referring to paragraph 39 to assist the Judges, Witness. There is nothing particular in there for you. But it's right that you give the impression of a power struggle between those three?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the question, a power struggle did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the differences between, first of all, Goran Hadzic and Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The differences were of a political nature. With respect to certain political matters, their views differed, and they were constantly quarrelling. Babic frequently accused Goran of not doing his work properly, that he was supported by Belgrade and that was the only reason he was in power, whereas Goran accused Babic of various things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it in the way that they went about their business or political differences between the two?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were political differences, and these were only reflected on their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so how would you express that political difference in a simple form as the difference between Hadzic and Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the basic political difference between them, if I can call it that, was that Babic advocated the position that Krajina should pursue an independent policy, whereas Goran Hadzic believed that we should rely more on our motherland, that is Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to Milan Martic, he also had differences with the other two. What was his different position, if you could describe that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference between Martic and Babic, in my judgement, was similar to the difference between Hadzic and Babic. Martic also felt that we should rely more on the motherland, and Babic the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the difference between Martic and Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there were no political differences between them. Both held the same position, but Martic was more critical of Hadzic in the sense of him being unable to do his work properly, that he wasn't serious enough, whereas Hadzic accused Martic of being a mere policeman who shouldn't get involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These political differences between the three made it very difficult, did it not, for there to be any settled or unified front within the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to work under those circumstances in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All three were operating different levers of power and working often against each other.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that was not in the best interests of the region or the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When it came to the Erdut agreement in 1995, you signed that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. agreement, and it achieved from that moment a peace and end to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You signed that -- that agreement to avoid further war with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having the experiences of the lower part of Krajina in mind when Martic wouldn't accept or negotiate, not to mention sign the Z4 plan, which I think was a major error for the people of Krajina, I had no other option but to get the most we could by peaceful means, and that was the agreement. And its greatest positive side was that the solution was a peaceful one, and the people would have the time of one year plus another year to be able to decide themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you signed that agreement and after you assigned that agreement, the local politicians and others were hostile to you. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly all, that is five presidents of municipalities, as many as there were in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and Goran Hadzic were against the agreement. However, after protracted persuasion, they agreed to it. But after the signature was affixed, I was attacked with heavy cannon to leave as soon as possible, and I left after the successful demilitarisation at the end of April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before you signed that agreement in Erdut, it was Slobodan Milosevic who told you to sign that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a message from Dayton from Mr. Milosevic, through Mr. Zika Jovanovic, who was then Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs, to the effect that President Milosevic said that it would be a good thing and that it should be done. However, from his closest associates - one could call them closest - I received opposite messages, that is that I shouldn't do it, and then I decided to do it nevertheless, because I knew that if I didn't do it on Saturday, that on Sunday the Croatian army would attack Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when Slobodan Milosevic returned from Erdut, he told you that you had done the right thing as he instructed, to sign the agreement for peace.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that I had done the right thing, and that was the only right thing to do, that the international community was putting great pressure on us, there was no other option. He asked me whether any of his men had criticised me. I said they hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To start with what Mr. Kay ended with, you said that you were -- the local politicians and Goran Hadzic acted hostile against you after the signing of the Erdut agreement. At that time after the signing of the Erdut agreement, did Mr. Milosevic support you against Goran Hadzic and the other local politicians that acted hostile against you or did he not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic knew about these attacks by Goran Hadzic and the other politicians against me after the signing of the agreement, and on several occasions he told me that, that various delegations were coming to see him and that they were complaining about me. And at first, I think he had a neutral position. I know that. That is true. But as time passed, the demilitarisation was completed, the main things had been done in the area; people had been disarmed, various units crossed into Serbia in plain clothes, and I think that most of the job had been done. Then, nevertheless, at a meeting he said that there were too many criticisms levelled against me, and the best thing for me to do would be to withdraw, to retire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you -- did he give you any explanation why he could not support you against those critics, or do you know why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but at the time, Mr. Milosevic was powerful, and I didn't ask him any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the budget of the RSK, Mr. Milosevic questioned you about the income from the oil fields. Was the crude oil sold for a realistic price or a lower price?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The oil was not sold as crude oil but in processed form at a low price. I remember roughly that this was around 30 pfennig; whereas, the market price, because there was an embargo and there was a blockade, it was sold at a price of between four and more marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who profited from this, selling the oil for such a low price?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially the oil was sold by the oil industry of Krajina. So that means that the company should have profited, but I believe that the people who purchased the oil at 30 or so pfennigs a litre and sold it at a higher price were the ones that profited.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And those people were where or who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were close to the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic asked you about the attack on Palaca. Was your village attacked by the villagers from Laslovo, or were they attacked by the ZNG forces from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the attack by Croatian forces on Palaca, I didn't know exactly who had attacked us, but after some time, I watched a Croatian officer who was bragging that this was in fact the first organised attack by the Croatian army against a locality, in this case Palaca, and it took place after an order by their command that they should move from Osijek via Vinkovci to Borovo Selo, and the operation was halted. They didn't attack Borovo Selo, but on the way back to Osijek, they attacked Palaca. According to what the Croatian officer who participated in the attack recounted himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic put to you that the leadership of Serbia always advocated and supported peace, and your answer to this proposition was that sometimes it was like that and sometimes it was not. Do you recall times or events when the Serbian leadership, in particular Mr. Milosevic, did not support peace?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MILANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question in concrete terms, but I'll give you an example. It is not logical for Milan Martic, who was supported by Belgrade all the years, that means for six years, in fact, it supported him for six years, and when it came to accepting the Z-4 plan, he did not accept it; whereas the extreme man, Babic, who had been considered such, strove for having the Z-4 plan accepted and later on signed it in Vienna, although the -- although Croatia had already launched an attack on that part of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter of housekeeping. I'm asked to note for the record that the original translation for Exhibit 551, tab 10, has been substituted by the new translation which we have all had today. Mr. Milanovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter before we adjourn. We will, in fact, adjourn before the next witness and take the break slightly early, and it is this, it involves all parties: We have to deal with the order and make arrangements for the hearing of the evidence of Lord Owen, and that will involve considering how long should be allowed for examination by the parties. I'm not going to ask for that now, but tomorrow I would be grateful to have some idea of how long the parties would wish to have for the -- his examination so we can make up an order. So we will discuss it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while we're on that subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- it's really how his evidence is presented. Will the Prosecution be asking him questions in chief, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I know he's a court witness. How is it going to be done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you were here with the last Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. court witness we had, Dr. Ranta.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was, but I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. In the same way, we'll start off with examination. We may consider inviting the witness, if he wants, to make a short statement, but we have his statement which is in written form. It will then be a question of cross-examination by all parties, and we will probably follow the same form as we did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's helpful to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the only issue we would welcome submissions on, we'll hear -- or, rather, we'll hear the parties on is how long they all want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now, 20 minutes, and then we'll start the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would first inquire regarding the motion, the 92 bis motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been granted and there's a written order which should be out by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could first begin by showing the witness the background sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is that your name on top of the piece of paper that you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is the information contained on that page correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd next ask that he be shown the 92 bis packet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If you could please look at that packet in front of you and tell us whether that is a packet that contains two statements of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you meet with a member of the registrar on the 15th of November of 2001 to certificate those statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I did?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At this time I'd ask that we have exhibit numbers for both the background sheet and the 92 bis packet and move both under seal into admission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pseudonym sheet is 554 under seal, and the Rule 92 bis statement is 554 -- 555 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a witness who lived most of his life in the Gornja Grapska, which is predominantly Muslim village in the municipality of Doboj. At the time that the conflict broke out in 1992, he was retired from a career as a professional policeman. His statements will tell you that the population of Doboj prior to the conflict was about 60.000 people, roughly divided equally between Muslims and Serbs. While the town of Doboj had a higher number of Muslims, most of the villages were Serb villages. His evidence, which is contained in the 92 bis statements, are broken down into two primary areas of interest. The first is with respect to the takeover of Doboj and the attack on his village. The second aspect of his statements refers to his time, his considerable amount of time in detention. With respect to the takeover of Doboj in February of 1992, a Muslim policeman from his village was given the task of establishing a reserve police unit in the village. These instructions came from headquarters in Doboj. The witness assisted in setting up this unit as he thought it would help stabilise a situation that was deteriorating and that it might assist in maintaining good relations with the police in Doboj town. The unit was comprised of reserve policemen, Muslim policemen from his village, and Serb reserve policemen from a neighbouring Serb hamlet. The reserve unit basically was to keep peace in the village. Two to three weeks after the unit was established, the Serb members of the unit said that they were prohibited from being part of this unit any more. They asked for and received their weapons, ammunition and equipment, and left the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The Serbs set up barricades in Doboj in mid-April of 1992. These were manned by local Serbs who were armed with professional military weapons. Two machine-guns were pointed at Gornja Grapska. From the time the barricades went up, the Muslims from this village were not permitted to pass through the village and were effectively cut off. On the 9th of May, 1992, six days after the town of Doboj was occupied, the witness and others in his village realised that they were about to be attacked as Serb paramilitary formations were gathering around the village. The villagers in his home tried to evacuate women, children, and elderly but were prohibited by armed Serbs from doing so. The Serb attack on Gornja Grapska took place on the 10th of May, 1992. The attacking Serbs wore JNA camouflage uniforms and were well-armed with professional JNA automatic rifles and weapons. Aside from some hunting rifles and other small arms, the villagers were unarmed. The witness did not hear a single shot being fired in defence of the village. The Serbs shelled the village throughout the day. During the shelling, 34 villagers were killed. These included men, women, and children. None the villagers were in military uniform. They were civilians. After the shelling of the village, the infantry attack started about 5.00 p.m. in the afternoon. This did not last very long as the Serbs came into the village unopposed. As he was led from his home one image that haunts this witness was seeing the lifeless body of a young 5-year-old child, lying with his eyes open. The residents were rounded up and went to a Serb village where the women and children were separated from the men and the men were detained. This leads to the second area of the substance of the witness's evidence. The witness was first detained in the warehouse at Bare. This was for approximately a week in May. He notes that they were treated like cattle, kicked and beaten. The facilities at Bare had been military hangars before the war. The witness was detained there and noted that approximately 1.200 people were kept there during the time he was there, and they were kept in these five hangars, each of which contained up to 300 men. The conditions in this facility were cruel. On the 18th of May, 1992, the witness and 27 other Muslim men were taken to the Spreca prison in Doboj. The witness would remain there until the 9th of February, 1993. Upon arrival, the prisoners were told that they were now in a Serbian state and that they could be treated as the Serbs wanted. The prisoners were beaten, humiliated and killed. Each of the eight cells in the facility usually housed approximately a hundred people. During the months that the witness was detained there, approximately 5.000 people passed through that prison. People came and left on a daily basis. During the entire time that he was there prisoners were taken out at night and then they would never be seen again. Whenever people were taken away, the witness and others would wonder if they would be the next ones. As bad as the physical torture at the prison was, the physical or the psychological anxiety was worse. At Spreca, the prisoners Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were taken out daily to do forced labour. Among the tasks that the witness performed was burying dead bodies. Another task was going through villages that had been taken over by the Serbs and removing anything of value so that the Serbs could take those items for themselves. In these villages, the witness saw civilian people who had been killed. Most of them were older and people who could not run away during the attack. Most of the witness's forced labour was at the JNA barracks in Doboj. These barracks were the headquarters of all military activities in the territory. The commander of this facility was a regular officer of the JNA. All the regular army units, reserve units, and paramilitary units operating in Doboj were based there. Among the paramilitary units that the witness saw there were the White Eagles, the Martic police, and the Knindza. On one occasion he saw approximately 300 local Serbs being trained by the Montenegrin Red Berets. The witness also noted that when units would come back after an unsuccessful battle, they would frequently abuse the detainees. On cleaning the barracks, the witness found blood and human teeth on the floor where people had been beaten. He noted that the JNA commanders were there throughout the entire time, saw all of this, and allowed it to happen. On the 9th of February, 1993, the witness was transferred with 40 others on a bus to a prison in Banja Luka. The detainees were told that they were being taken to be judged. At this prison, the detainees were taken out for interrogation regarding political matters. During the days the detainees were forced to sit without moving, without talking, on chairs from 7:00 in the morning until 7:00 at night. His detention in Banja Luka ended on about the 16th or 17th of May, 1993 when he was transported to Usora prison in Doboj. Again there were beatings and people disappearing at night. During this time, the witness worked at a local factory in Doboj as his forced labour. He was kept there until the 1st of October, 1993, when he was exchanged. During his time in detention, the witness lost approximately 25 kilogrammes. To this day, he still suffers the physical consequences of his detention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B-1115, I only have excepts from the documents. I know nothing about Doboj, so I'm going to ask you to clear some things up that were mentioned. You are testifying, as far as I was able to read from what I've been given and from what the brief summary stated, about the events in Doboj and about the suffering of the unprotected Muslims there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You speak about paramilitary formations and the Yugoslav People's Army in that respect.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know when the Yugoslav People's Army left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that things were the reverse and that the defence of Doboj during those war years was very difficult because Doboj was attacked practically from all sides, both by the Muslim and by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Doboj was not attacked either by the Muslim or by the Croatian forces, but on Sunday the 3rd of May, 1992, it was attacked by the Serb army, and that's how it was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say attacked by the Serb army, didn't Serbs live in Doboj? Weren't they there already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, they were there, but they were all wearing uniforms, all the military-able men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that throughout the time you're testifying about there were continuous attacks launched at Doboj, especially in 1992, from regular units from neighbouring Croatia as well as by paramilitary formations from Bosnia-Herzegovina, both Muslim and Croatian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I can't claim that that is not so, but I don't know whether it is or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that various paramilitary formations were established, Muslim and Croatian ones, precisely in the municipality of Doboj itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know anything about the attacks at the Serb forces in the Doboj area from the regions of neighbouring municipalities Gracanica, Zavidovici and Maglaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: That was not in May 1992. If it did happen, then when they started to take control of the towns and villages, then they were standing up to the BH army, and I assume that these conflicts broke out in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Gracanica, Maglaj and Zavidovici, are they neighbouring municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, Zavidovici is further away but Maglaj and Doboj, yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the Muslim forces in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it from Gracanica that they attacked Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I don't know what they could have attacked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean they could have attacked with? With weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I was exchanged in 1993, on the 1st of October, and when I reached the Gracanica area and when I looked at the members -- saw the members of the BH army there, quite simply - and believe me when I say this - I felt fear, because I had come from an area, as I was travelling to be exchanged, I encountered vast artillery weapons ranging from tanks and other artillery pieces, and I was very much afraid when I crossed over to that region because I thought, "Well, I'll probably be killed here." And when I looked to the other side, there were just a few sporadic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say there were just sporadic rifles, do you remember when the so-called Patriotic League was first formed, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I can't know that, because at that time I was incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was established quite a long time before you were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I must say that I retired before the war, I was a pensioner, and went about my own business as such, and I was loyal to my household. I wasn't interested in any parties or the Patriotic League or one side or another. All I did was work for myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you say that it was only sometime in May that you were exposed to these conflicts, do you happen to know that during that period of time, the one you're testifying about, the Muslim forces and the Croatian forces to all intents and purposes had taken control of all major towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Except for the Doboj, which was encircled and a part of Sarajevo and the town of Banja Luka, which was in a relatively secure Serb encirclement, all the other larger towns were practically in the hands of the Patriotic League and the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer that question. All I can say is that I don't know how they could have fallen into the hands of the Patriotic League and other units that you mentioned. I don't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're a man who worked in a state organisation. You were a policeman, you had a certain amount of education and training. So the largest towns that I mentioned, the university centres in Bosnia and Herzegovina, apart from Banja Luka which was mostly populated by the Serbs, and Sarajevo, the greatest part of it, Mostar, Tuzla, and the other three university centres and the largest industrial centres as well, all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of them were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO; isn't that right? Is it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I should like to emphasise once again that I don't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know anything about the time when the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: All I know is the time it spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and those imprints have stayed to the present day on me, on my environment. But when it pulled out, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A moment ago, as you yourself said, and it was also mentioned in paragraph 14 of your statement, that in February 1992, a policeman by the name of Refik Buljubasic from your village was given the assignment of establishing a reserve police unit in your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that that order was received by him from the headquarters in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And later on, when I was able to analyse all this in greater detail, I came to the knowledge that, nonetheless, all the members of the police force who were Muslims were dealt with in the same way at the police station in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "dealt with"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, they wanted only Serbs to remain in the police station in Doboj and all the Muslims allegedly should set up in their local communities some sort of police stations of mixed composition, and yes it was a mixed composition up to a certain period of time when they received orders that they had to withdraw from the -- withdraw and separate. So they then took their weapons, ammunition, and we never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you helped Refik Buljubasic to establish that unit made up of reserve policemen; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this reserve unit had as its task to maintain law and order in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, law and order in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any unrest in the village and did the police have to intervene? Is that what they did, to have a police force concentration in the village? What was the reason for that? What was happening in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: The police unit set up in my own native village had as its assignment and task to keep the peace, to establish law and order and prevent any crimes from being committed within their own ethnic group. However, this was a formality, and there were few incidents, maybe in coffee bars when the youngsters would have a little too much to drink, alcoholic drink, but this was all negligible and more or less normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no unrest in your village, and yet this unit was set up. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, we could say that there was no unrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many members did that unit have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Approximately 36 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So a 36-man unit was established in the village in which there was no unrest. Well, wasn't this a question of an obvious paramilitary formation being formed in the village? Wasn't that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: You mean the reserve police unit that was established?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean this 30-odd man unit set up in a village in which you said was mostly inhabited by Muslims, there was no unrest, and yet a unit, as you yourself say, was formed of about 30 people or more. Isn't that a paramilitary formation, a paramilitary unit formed in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is true that a police -- a reserve police unit was established, however, what I wish to say is it is easy to draw a conclusion now and say that it was a paramilitary formation, but there were Serb members of the reserve police force. Then it wasn't a paramilitary force. Then once they withdrew, suddenly it was characterised as being a paramilitary formation. How come?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. That's when they were termed in this way. I understood from what you said that in your -- your village was inhabited by Muslims alone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: The majority population in my village was Muslim, that is true, but it was divided into two parts. One district was more numerous, and that was the Muslim populated district. And the other district was inhabited by the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And the unit that was established in your village, that is to say in the Muslim part of your village, these several members who were Serbs were actually from the neighbouring settlement as you said, or district; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, it's the same area. It's just 20 or 30 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were not actually from your village but from the immediate vicinity, and then they left you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No. They were from my village. It was an united village, and we were always registered and classed as a united village, one village in all the documents. But in addition to the Serb members of the reserve police unit, there were active-duty policemen as well. It wasn't only a reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I assume that there was an active policeman here and there, but before the events unfolded, was there any police unit in the village at all before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Reserve police force. That means civilians sitting at home that might be reservists, but there was no police in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, no regular police, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, overnight suddenly as you yourself said, there was a group of some 30 armed men appearing in your village; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No. It's not a group. It's a registered reserve police station armed by the police station in Doboj. You know that police station was not formed then, it was formed before, some 20 years ago. There were reservists as members who had up to 15 and 20 years of service who had their own weapons on them which were never taken away from them until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the JNA was pulling out of Bosnia and the Serbs in the meantime did not manage to organise their own defence, is it true that in opposition -- as opposed to them, there was a large number of paramilitary units in those socio-political communities consisting of Muslims and Croats in the TO in Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I can only talk about my own settlement where I lived as a pensioner. I didn't move around much. I took care of my own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Though you acted in that way and you were in this unit and you helped Refik Buljubasic to form it, already at the beginning of 1992, virtually in all municipalities there wasn't a municipality without a smaller or larger unit of the Patriotic League, the National Guards Corps, the Green Berets, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we did go through this. It was not the first witness. There may have been a great many. You've heard his answer. He can only deal with his own area. You choose then to ask him general questions and a great deal of time is wasted. He's told you he can't answer. He can deal with his own area specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware in your area, precisely because of the existence of all these formations that came into being at the time, that is in 1992, there were large casualties among the Serbs, the largest being in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I'd just like to know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
