utterances.text: For instance, in your own municipality of Doboj. Do you have any idea about the environment in Doboj and how many victims there were among the Serbs in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must address you and say believe me, I have nothing to do with any of that. I never heard of that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard nothing about fighting around Doboj and the battlefield around Doboj, Ozren, and this whole region and things that were happening there, very intensified combat during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: If you're talking about the beginning of the war, then you must understand that for 520 days or for 17 months, almost 18, I was in the hands of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's see what you do know. You say that the Serbs set up barricades in Kostajnica. Kostajnica is a part of Doboj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, a suburb of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that they set up the barricade in April 1992. You say that there were two machine-gun nests there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those machine-guns were pointed towards Gornja Grapska, so you were unable to reach Doboj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Towards Gornja Grapska and the right bank of the Bosna River and the plains along that route. So it was not possible to leave my native village and go in the direction of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the road led through the woods and hills towards Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes. Those are dirt roads through the woods that I used to use as a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who controlled those roads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: It was controlled by the army -- rather, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that it was in 1992, precisely in April, in the town of Doboj itself the Muslims started erecting barricades and prevented communications and supplies reaching the population and prevented safe local and transit traffic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I must add in connection with that road that led towards Gracanica, and you could also take it to go to Doboj, that eight of our civilians were captured. They had tried to leave this hell, and they were captured. Out of the eight, all were taken to prison. Four came out, and four of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 16 that on the 8th of April, eight persons tried to escape by this route. They were arrested and taken to the Spreca prison in Doboj, and four of them were later killed. The other four were liberated later on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: That's what I just said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How do you know that these four were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I know. First of all, there is no trace of them to this day. Secondly, one of the four was found in Slavonski Brod after the war when mass graves were exhumed, and through a DNA analysis it was established that he was one of the eight. When they killed those men, the Serbian army, when carrying out exchanges with Croatia across the Sava River at Slavonski Brod, they would give those men in black body bags to be exchanged, and now that the dust has settled, it has become clear that this one was one of the eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the data and information I have in these documents, when the dead were exchanged, it was those who were killed in battle that were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I just pointed out that this was a case in the area of Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How do you know that those eight who were trying to break through, that four of them were not killed during the attempted breakthrough and the other four captured? But rather, you claim that eight were captured and four of them killed. Couldn't it be the other way round?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: When you say "breakthrough," it's not a breakthrough. People were trying to leave their village because their lives were in danger. Now, whether they were killed in battle, then these other four who were released and who are free and who are all over Europe, they say that it was as I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those eight who were going along that road, are you claiming that they were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, unarmed. I know all eight of those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say on page 4, in the first paragraph, which begins on page 4, and you say: "In my first statement, on page 2 I refer to a delegation which went to Busletic. Some days before that, the same delegation went to see Boro Paravac who was staying at his brother's house in Kostajnica."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "He had invited us there to tell us not to make any problems for the military convoys coming through our village." So you had an armed unit in the village, and they are making arrangements with you not to cause problems, because if you didn't have an armed unit in the village, you couldn't cause problems to the convoys that were passing through.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: That is true that Mr. Boro Paravac told a delegation not to view the Yugoslav army in the same way. That is, the Serbs and the Muslims did not view the Yugoslav army in the same way. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you stop convoys, open fire at convoys? Why did he call you to warn you if you hadn't done any of those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I don't know who could have fired with the exception of the reserve police that were armed. No one else had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well -- very well. Those 30 men in your village who were armed, did they fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: They didn't dare appear on the main road along which the Serbian army and paramilitary units were passing. These were enormous APCs, whole convoys of people, large convoys. On the contrary, they opened fire at shops, coffee bars, homes. So they frightened the civilian population. I must say that people no longer stayed in their houses because of these convoys passing by. They moved away from the main road as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, do you know of the barricade that you - and when I say "you" I don't mean you personally, I mean your forces - erected in the villages of Jokovac and Seslije, cutting off road traffic towards Derventa and Modrica? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I would add that Croatian inhabitants live in that area. But Boro Paravac cautioned us regarding our behaviour towards the Serb army, because when they were waging war in Brod and around Brod and in the area of Modrica, all the wounded and all the materiel and the troops had to move towards Doboj and had to secure the road to the hospital, because where you mentioned the barricades I don't know because I wasn't there, but probably they couldn't move in that direction because it's the same road leading to Doboj like the one going along the left bank of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Brod. Do you know that in the area of Brod, the village of Sijekovac, a massacre was committed against the Serbs long before these conflicts that you are testifying about started? This is close to you; you must have known about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: It is some 50-odd kilometres away from me, you see. And I want to say in that connection that I heard about it after the war, on television when there were certain programmes broadcast, that this event had happened in Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: On the basis of the stories of the parents of those young men killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was killed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I don't know who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were the victims Serbs or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: If the Serbs are saying that they lost their children, then they couldn't have been anything but Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that, really. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, did tension increase in the broader area including Doboj, after this massacre in a place that you say is 50 kilometres away from yours? That's not so far.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: It's not too far, but I must repeat, this did not interest me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's your affair that it didn't interest you. And do you know that before these events, you said that on the 9th of May there were conflicts in Doboj and that you were attacked on the 10th, that as early as the 4th of April, a month prior to this, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, without Serb representatives, took a decision to mobilise the TO, the police, the Civil Defence, even though Bosnia and Herzegovina was still a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I do know that it was a part of Yugoslavia, but I don't know that a decision was taken to form such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in 1992, on the 12th of April -- surely you remember that. You were free then and you were still in your village. So this is six days after the recognition of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina Alija Izetbegovic ordered an all-out attack on the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you are talking about the events of the 9th and 10th of May, according to my information, and I would like to ask you kindly just to say whether that is correct or not. On the 3rd of May, that is six days prior to the 9th, units of the army and police removed barricades and other obstacles put up in Doboj and organised by the SDA and HDZ leaderships, and these obstacles, due to which Serb parts of the town were isolated and facilities of significance, for instance, the road leading to the hospital and other important institutions in town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: At that time, I was not in Doboj, and I also don't know which barricades. I don't know when the town was attacked militarily on the 3rd of May, 1992. It was a Sunday, and the civilians that were left fled in great haste. I don't know what barricades and where those barricades were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 3rd of May, the army and the police removed the barricades erected by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to repeat. There were no barricades there. But I repeat, Serb forces on that day, a Sunday, the 3rd of May, 1992, attacked the town of Doboj with great force from all sides so that all the non-Serb population fled to save their lives. They fled their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is probably taken out of some context. Do you know, please tell me, that on the 6th of May, regular units of Croatia attacked and killed Serb inhabitants in the village of Vitusica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I'm not going to claim that they didn't, but I don't know anything about that, because by then, I was already surrounded, and I could have no contact with anyone outside my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about that. Yet all those are events that took place before this 9th and 10th of May that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, I'm sure you know that that is St. George's Day, an Orthodox holiday, and the patron saint of many Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Perhaps. It is not my family feast day, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was precisely on the 6th of day -- on the 6th of May for St. George's Day that the Croatian forces killed the Serb population in this village, that is to say three days prior to the events that you describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am saying that that is possible. However, I do not know about it. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that apart from this attack and the killing of the people and the looting and setting fire to the houses, in addition to Vitusica, the village of Brezik in the Doboj municipality and Majevac, a neighbouring village in the Doboj municipality, suffered that fate? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: The villages Mr. Milosevic has mentioned to me are familiar but during the war because they took us there on some work assignments. We had to do some farming there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you were there, then I'm sure you have heard about the other man called Milos Milenko Savetic, the Savetic family, and all their houses were set on fire precisely on the 6th of May, just three days prior to the events you're describing, and this was done by the formations that stormed the Doboj municipality and set fire to the houses and killed the people in Ritesice, Brezik, Majevac and all these places. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I have to say I don't know about that, and you're talking about it now; I have not mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a single name of somebody who was killed, of the people who were killed there? I am asking you. I'm not saying you said it, I'm just asking you whether you know any of the people who were killed on that attack on the 6th of May, any of their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, roughly, I know that the surrounding parts, that there were -- that there was general disagreement in the environs but that somebody killed someone and I know their names and surnames, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember of another event in which a man named Mirko Dejanovic from Majevac went to Ritesice to take over the body of a neighbour who had been killed, by the name of Popovic, in order to bury his body? But he was also killed in a very brutal manner; his head was cut off with a pickax. So this was an event which everybody knew about who lived in those parts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say that I really don't know about that event. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Jela Titura, does that name ring a bell, from Vitusica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No. Well, it's quite a long way off from where I was. I just passed through those parts on rare occasions, so I really don't know the people who lived there, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move to some more specific points in your statement. From paragraphs 15 and 16, in which you stated that the regular military formations, the reserve and paramilitary units in Doboj were stationed in the barracks in the village of Miljkovac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say they slept there, ate there, underwent training there, and went into battle from there. That's what you say in paragraph or point 12.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please explain this to me: If your village was cut off from Doboj, how then were you able to see all this? How were you able to see the paramilitary units, the White Eagles, the Martic's men, the Tigers, the Knindzas, and all the others that you mention? How were you able to see them coming in? And yet when I ask about the massacres of the Serb population in the Serb villages, you say you were under siege and knew nothing. How were you able to see this if you were under a blockade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Please allow me to explain. With respect to these assertions and what I stated, I stand by. What I want to say is that during that time, for about five months or 150 days, every day continuously, nonstop, I spent time at the 4th of July barracks. I worked there. I helped move certain officers, I did some gardening, looked after the flowers and the shrubs and painted some fences there where the army underwent training. So I was there the whole time. So everything I wrote down in my statement is what I saw. They're all things that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1115. You've just explained that you tended the flowers and painted the fences and things of that kind. A moment ago, you explained to us that you collected up bodies, teeth that had been bashed out. So tell us what you did in fact do. You have to choose. Was -- did that come under the tending of the garden, the shrubs and flowers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I did that and so did the other detainees, all those incarcerated with me. We dug graves for the dead. We also tended to the flowers and flowerbeds and even worked on private Serb property. We would dig around the corn fields and collect up the hay and cut up logs for winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've enumerated a great deal of tasks that you had; tending to the flowers and the maize and making haystacks, you did farming, you buried bodies. But this doesn't seem to -- the first lot of tasks doesn't seem to go with the next lot of tasks, the gathering and burying of bodies, of corpses. Where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: When I went to the barracks, other people went with me. We all went round these places, all the detainees. Sometimes I would go, sometimes we would all go. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1115. You're the first man who says he saw in Bosnia-Herzegovina some kind of Montenegrin Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They trained some 300 of them. Do you know that this unit, a Montenegrin Red Beret unit never existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: It was the Serb Montenegrin berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1115. You're the first man who has talked to us about Montenegrin Red Berets. You also say that your reserve police unit -- although you didn't consider it to be a paramilitary formation, did you, Mr. 1115?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, we did not. We had no intention of establishing that kind of unit, and we didn't treat it, therefore, as a paramilitary unit either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you say that on the 10th of May, there was an attack on your village and this was led by a man called Stankovic from the Yugoslav People's Army, the attack on your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, Milovan Stankovic personally, a major of the Yugoslav People's Army, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how were you able to come by that conclusion? Did you learn about that later on, information to that effect once -- or were you able to establish who attacked you when the attack was launched and who was in command and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: That same evening when we were evacuated from the village, I saw him standing in front of the tank at the entrance to the village. And one year later, when I happened to return from Banja Luka, we went to cut some logs at Mount Ozren, and he was there. And then he told me personally that he was one of the men who was the main responsible person in command of the forces that launched the attack on my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that on the 11th of May, for instance, the last JNA units pulled out of the Bosanski Brod municipality, and the withdrawal started long before that. So there couldn't have been a JNA unit there on the 10th of May in your village. And then you also say at 1700 hours, which means towards evening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. You're trying to put two points to the witness. The allegation, Witness B-1115, the suggestion is the JNA couldn't have been there because they were supposed to have withdrawn earlier or that sort of thing. Were the JNA present in the village that day during the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then explain this to me. Explain what you wrote in paragraph 18, I think it is -- or, rather, the third paragraph on page 4 in which you say: "The attack on my village began on the 10th of May, 1992, and was carried out by the Serbs from the area of Ozren."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I read out the whole sentence to you. That means that the attack on your village on the 10th of May, 1992, according to your claims, and you are testifying on the basis your statement, not live testimony, was carried out by the Serbs from the Ozren area. And then you go on to say: "Stankovic was their commander."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on what grounds -- you say that they wore camouflage JNA uniforms, that they were well-armed. All right. But you said that they were Serbs from the Ozren area, not members of the JNA. You say that in the sentence before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: According to what I know, Stankovic was an active-duty officer of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he was from the Ozren area, this man Stankovic, then he was the commander of the army of Republika Srpska in the Ozren area and not a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: That's what he could have been. That's possible. That's what I can assume he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So not even in your statement do you say that you were actually attacked by the JNA. You just say that the attack was carried out by Serbs from the area of Ozren, and Ozren is a mountain near Doboj; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that the Serbs launched that attack from that mountain on your village, and now you claim that that attack was launched by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I have to say, Your Honours, if I may that on the 11th of May, 1992, when I arrived at the Vuk Karadzic Primary School by the station, I spent the night there with the other inhabitants from my own native place, and the next day they lined us up in the training grounds, and that's when I saw that there was still some members of the JNA there, because my son used to study. He was a -- he studied at the military academy in the Belgrade, and he was standing right next to 1993 there and he said, "Father, that man over there that came out of that military unit, his name is Ozegovic [phoen], and he was a professor at the academy. He taught defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you've been talking about an attack launched by Serbs from the Ozren area, do you still stand by the assertion and claim that that attack was an attack against your village at all and that it was carried out by the JNA? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: In combined with the JNA. In combined formation with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Because some professor from the academy who was probably from the area was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes. He was a professor, but he was also an officer of the JNA, a lieutenant colonel, in fact, by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was what he had been before, but is he originally from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No. I'd never seen or heard of him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Never seen or heard of him before that. Right. Now, do you know that it was precisely whole Serb villages in that area that were left empty? There were no more inhabitants because they had taken refuge in the face of the attacks I described a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain that, but those villages, they weren't evacuated, the population anywhere. On the 9th of May, in fact, one day prior to the attack on my native village, we wanted to leave the village, all of us to leave the village. However, the neighbouring village which was Serb populated did not allow us to leave. They returned us all back to my native village so that they could attack us the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the Serb village didn't allow you to leave? You mean somebody from some of the units of the army of Republika Srpska blocked the exit and didn't allow you to pass; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that the problem of refugees was vast? Their accommodation and food for them in Doboj where people had taken refuge from the empty villages in the face of the slaughter that was carried out against them and that this was an enormous problem for the leadership, both for the civilian leadership and the military leadership, the vast number of refugees from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Perhaps that is so, but I was incarcerated myself at the time, so I wasn't able to see or control the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that because of the withdrawal of the JNA, there was the danger of Doboj finding itself in an encirclement and under siege from the Muslim and Croatian forces, that it be completely blocked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I don't know why it would have been under siege. What weapons would they have used to form an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned yourself a moment ago that you had heard a long time before the events took place that the events happened in Brod, Sijekovac, where a regular brigade, in fact, killed the Serb population there, and that was the first organised storming by organised formations on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and crimes committed against the Serbs en masse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Perhaps that is so, but I don't want to enter into that because I don't know about it. What I'm talking about is about my native village and the defence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that there was a defence line set up for Doboj along the River Bosna for the defence? Do you know about that? In May that that was set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was thought that a breakthrough would be a catastrophe for the local population and the Serb refugees and that with great effort the road via Grapska was deblocked, Predrovo, Modrica and Vucak, in fact, that road? All that had been blocked previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they deblocked that axis, that road, precisely through your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to say that my village, about a month before the aggression against it, had already been surrounded. We had no communications. We were cut off. We knew nothing that was happening in Doboj and its environments, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that this wasn't an attack, it was the deblocking in order to prevent a complete blockade, because that was the communication road from Doboj via Grapska, Predrovo and Modrica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already answered that. He doesn't know. Now, you've got about six minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to get through everything in six minutes, Mr. May. I do realise that it seems to you that the only priority is time, the time factor, but I do have to ask certain questions. Now, you can, of course, take away that right. It's your right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, do you remember that during those days the Muslim units launched an attack on Vijenac, which is one of the most important elevations on Mount Ozren, of greatest significance to the defence of the Serb forces? Otherwise it is a Serb populated area. Isn't that right, Mr. 1115?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You complain about -- you complain about not having sufficient time. All you do in these cross-examinations is not to challenge the evidence of the witnesses but to put a contrary complaint about what you allege the Muslims did to the Serbs. Now, that goes on in every cross-examination. We don't know, because you haven't challenged so far, whether you accept or not that 34 civilians were killed in the attack. That's what you should be concentrating on, dealing with what the witness said, not a series of contrary allegations which, as you know, is not a defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An opposite claim denies the claim which is opposite to it, or maybe I don't understand things correctly. I do not have information that there was attack on Grapska. What I do have information is that there was a deblockade of this route towards Predrovo and Vucak because Doboj was threatened by a total blockade, and I'm asking the witness about the attack on Vijenac, which was a very important feature for the defence of Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us about that? It's an alleged there was an attack on Vijenac. An attack by Muslim forces on the Serbs. Was there such an attack, as far as you know, or not, or can't you help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Hazim Dzinic, for instance, a Muslim, in a newspaper Nasi Dani, in Zenica, on the 23rd of September, 1992, on page 7, described the battles waged at the end of April 1992 in the ensettlement of Mahala above Doboj when, as he says, for two days and two nights the Muslims inflicted heavy losses on the Serb side. Does this mean anything to you? Because that is what he described in these words. Are you familiar with this? This is the end of April 1992. The settlement is Mahala, above Doboj. For two nights and two days the Muslims inflicted heavy losses on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: The gentleman you mention, who is a doctor of law, Hazim Dzinic, is somebody I know very well. He passed away recently. And what you are mentioning is something I really have no idea about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he passed away recently, that doesn't mean that in September 1992, in the paper I have mentioned and the page I have given you, he didn't say what I said. So you don't know anything about it, though you're from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of Zevudin Zonic [phoen], Mensur Brkic, and Kresimir Zubak? This is the TO command which was in control of these operations at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Among the three, I only know Kresimir Zubak, who worked in the prosecutor's office in Doboj before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that they planned the evacuation of the population towards Tesanj? And this was done at the beginning of May, that is the 8th of May, when certain separation lines were formed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: If we're talking about the beginning of May, the only conclusion one can draw is that the remaining inhabitants - the sick, the elderly - could only be evacuated from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Your own newspaper, Oslobodjenje, on the 11th of May, 1992, which means that it was written on the 10th of May and not later if the date of publication is the 11th of May, and it says on page 3: The Serbs have to be expelled from Doboj, and I quote: "Assessments from the battlefield indicate that by the end of the month, in view of the advances made by defence units, the whole area between Bosanski Brod and Doboj will be cleansed of the Serbs." This was stated in your newspaper on the 11th of May, and as newspaper is printed the day before it comes out, that the whole area from Doboj to Brod, including Doboj and Brod, had to be cleansed of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: If you're referring to the 11th of May, on the 11th of May, 1992, I was fighting for my own survival and that of my family who were with me. There were minor children with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about large-scale battles, and that your side envisaged that you would win all those battles and capture Doboj and Brod and the whole area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You have been asking this witness for a great deal of time about matters which he has not been able to answer. Now, it is pointless to waste the time of the Tribunal in this way. You will have the opportunity, as you know, to put forward your own case about events in this municipality, but there is no point going on asking the witness about things and putting reports to him when he says he doesn't know, and his answer to that question was he did not know. He was fighting for his own survival at the time. Now, that's his answer. Now, we have to get on. Now, you've got one more question if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. May, but I would ask you to give me a little more time for me to put several more questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can ask one more question. You know the rules with these witnesses. You've got one hour, so you must use it to the best advantage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1115, you say that the Serbs organised detention places or prisons for the Muslim and Croat inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that those prisons had existed before, such as places of temporary detention? Those were no special prisons for Muslims and Croats but for everyone who is in violation of the law, that kill people, set up ambushes and block traffic. They are not prisons for Muslims and Croats but for all who violate the law.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: In my statement, the places indicated where the camps were, one of them is a prison that before the war was a prison for the Doboj region. However, under normal conditions, as I had access to those prisons, I am familiar with the premises, there were beds there, and there was sufficient space for moving around. However, during the war, the beds were taken out, some sponge mattresses were thrown in, and people were crowded so that up to three men had to use a single metre-wide sponge bed. Only Croats and Bosniaks. Not a single Serb was in the prison at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many men were in the prison at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: I can say that at least 5.000 people passed through that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And for each of those 5.000 men, you can claim that not a single one was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the last question. Yes, could you deal with that? Could you give your answer, please? Of the 5.000 men you're asked, can you claim that not a single one was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stayed in room 65341, in those premises. Maybe there are another two or three that I didn't mention. And there wasn't a single Serb in those rooms. They were only Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your statement, Witness, you refer to JNA barracks in Doboj. I'm looking at paragraph 12 and paragraph 13. Were those barracks existing places of the JNA? Had they been bases of the JNA for many years previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Likewise, the JNA barracks in Sevarlije?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: An existing barracks before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1115
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I just ask you to have admitted into evidence the document I received from the side opposite? I cannot read out the name of the witness as he's a protected witness, but there is his name here, his father's name, and this is a document showing that he was charged under Article 124 of the Penal Code for armed insurrection as stated here. In translation I can't find it in the original written by hand, yes it says, "oruzana pubuna," or armed insurrection. Article 124 of the Penal Code. So could it be exhibited as I received it from the opposite side? So I assume they will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 02127552 -- no. 02127551.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where his name is mentioned. And the translation doesn't have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a copy if we have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Our copies are upstairs, Your Honour. I have one with me that I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we could just have a look at that one. Thank you. All is well. We've got one from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. B-1115, this is the -- you've heard what the accused has read out, and the suggestion that you were charged with armed insurrection. Do you know anything about that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you please just briefly deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This reserve force, all of those who had long barrels, each and every one of them were charged with armed insurrection, and we went to court several times in Banja Luka and Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply we were interrogated by the court, and it was difficult. The worst part was getting there. We would come across soldiers. They would beat us. But nothing really, apart from that dead member who according to the authorities of Republika Srpska or, rather, the military authorities, we were allegedly some sort of organisers of an armed insurrection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there a trial, B-1115?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this document with the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 194, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bibles, if you've got any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I have no redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness B-1115, that does conclude your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, we're going to deal with this. We've just been given a series of documents which I think are the admissions, what have been admitted under Rule 92 bis. Perhaps you can help us with it. We'll deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Those are the bundle of statements and -- sorry, transcripts that were admitted without cross-examination on the Brcko 92 bis (D) application. So that is what you have before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will -- you and the registry must go through these and give them the rightful numbers. Have you got your bundle there, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you and the registry, between you, will give the numbers to them now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 92 bis package for B-1407 will be 556. The 92 bis package for 1408 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt the registrar. The first tab in that Exhibit number 556 should be under seal, just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness B-1408 92 bis package will be 557. That's a repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And also could the first tab of that be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness B-1411 will be 558.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could tabs 1 and 2 of that exhibit number be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibits for Dr. Albert Charles Hunt will be 559. 92 bis package for B-1450 will be 560.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can tabs 1 and 2, both tabs, be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do we have under number 556?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 556, Your Honour, is Witness Exhibit B-1407 [sic]. And, Your Honour, for Exhibit 558 -- the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we received one for 1407?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you're going to call the next witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is B-1445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: After the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the 92 bis package be passed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness B-1445, can you look at the document at the front of that package and confirm, please, that you see your name upon that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes. This one here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, did you sign a declaration on the 29th of April, 2003, certifying that earlier statements that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor were true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the 92 bis package could be admitted as this witness's first exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Exhibit number will be 561 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Could the witness be handed, please, the bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, look at tab 1, please, in front of you. Is that the front sheet of an additional statement signed by you on the 13th of October of this year in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, do you comment in that statement upon documents shown to you in The Hague and upon two intercepts that were played to you whilst you were in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that that additional statement obtained whilst the witness was in The Hague and disclosed to the accused on the 13th of October, two nights ago, along with the associated exhibits referred to in that statement contained in your binder at tabs 2 and following be admit under Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's, just -- the statement. So this is the first time, of course, we've seen it. The statement is one of 11 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's producing, is it, exhibits which haven't been referred to before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but disclosed under -- pursuant to 65 ter but disclosed again to the accused on the 13th of October, i.e., two afternoons ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that the right way to deal with this - I speak for myself - since this is new material, is for the exhibit to be admitted but for the witness to go through these documents so we know what there are, briefly, and give his evidence live about it. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, these are new documents being introduced at a very late stage which, although they may have been in the 65 ter material, bore no relation, of course, to the witness statement of this particular witness within that material and would have just been documents existing within many several tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands. Time should be given to the accused to be able to digest this material and understand exactly what is happening here as it's plainly a new approach by the Prosecutor in relation to this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit the statement subject to this, that the witness must go through these exhibits, dealing with them insofar as they are of significance and pointing out the matters relied on so the Prosecution could know -- so the Court can know what it is the Prosecution seek to rely on these witnesses in these statements. Meanwhile, the accused will begin his cross-examination today, but he won't have to finish it today, and he will have the opportunity overnight of considering any matters and preparing for cross-examination on the documents. I should say that any intercepts which are appearing in the documents can only be admitted marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack. Perhaps we could have a new number for the next package, as it were, the statement and the attached exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be 562.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll read a short summary of the earlier statement testimony. This witness, a Muslim and of Bosniak ethnicity, was born and lived in Doboj until the war broke out. He gives evidence about the importance of Doboj as a strategic town, the number of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats in the municipality, and life in the town before the war broke out. He gives evidence about the locations and number of JNA army barracks in and around Doboj town. The witness speaks to the results of the 1990 elections in Doboj and the leadership in Doboj following those elections. He describes the members of the Council for National Defence for the municipality. He gives evidence about the SDS party in Doboj and the presence of Radovan Karadzic, Velibor Ostojic and Nikola Koljevic in Doboj at a pre-election rally in August or September 1990. The witness saw Karadzic on a further occasion in Doboj when he came to participate in a meeting the SDS were holding in secret. In early 1992, the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina formed their own parliament. From that time, the SDS in Doboj no longer cooperated in the Municipal Assembly. Incidents began to take place in Doboj against Bosniaks. Two or three months before the war, the SDS established a Crisis Staff in Doboj. Even in the period after the 1990 elections, the SDS had paramilitary units which practised on Mount Ozren. The witness describes the transformation of the JNA to a one-nationality army when the war started in Croatia in 1991 and the distribution of weapons to Serb civilians. In January or February 1992, units of Arkan's paramilitary and Seselj's White Eagles arrived in Doboj. About 20 days before the war started, reserve army units established checkpoints manned by local Serb soldiers on all roads leading into and out of town. The Serbs took control of Doboj on the 3rd of May, 1992. The Bosniaks were not prepared for military action and did not have any weapons to defend themselves. The witness moved out of Doboj with others on the 3rd of May, 1992. He moved to Tesanj and remained there until the Dayton Agreement was sign. He has since 1996 returned to Doboj several times. The witness was elected as a member of the Assembly of Republika Srpska on the 10th of August, 2000. Does the witness have in front of him a 92 bis package?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, could you turn, please, in the 92 bis package or could the witness be shown his first statement. Witness, turn, please, to paragraph 18 of your first statement to the OTP. That's dated the 26th of January, 1999. That's paragraph 18 of the B/C/S version. Witness, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about the matters you speak to in that paragraph. You talk about the presence of Arkan's paramilitaries and Seselj's White Eagles in Doboj. Did you personally see Arkan's men in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I didn't see them personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you personally watch the arrival of Arkan's and Seselj's men in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Not at that moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you see Seselj's paramilitaries in town at a later time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where you saw them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I saw them in front of the Serb Orthodox Church, at the entrance to the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Were you told by others how many there were in town and, if so, please tell us how many.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: According to the Muslim population with respect to the Serb residents who have their flats, they called me several times and said that in the presence of a large number of soldiers or, rather, Seselj's radicals, and I passed by that part of town only once because it was very dangerous, and I saw at the door or, rather, at the entrance to the courtyard five or six soldiers, Seselj's.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Please turn now to paragraph 22 of the statement. Look at paragraphs 22 and 23. Did you yourself witness the takeover of Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you leave Doboj on the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Are the matters stated in paragraphs 22 and 23 matters about which you learned from people who later fled Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: In paragraph 23, yes, I saw Seselj's paramilitary units completely in a place called Ankare, which is a weekend settlement where some 15 days prior to that they had expelled all the owners of the weekend holiday homes and to all intents and purposes occupied that area, and they were there up until the 3rd of May or, rather, they held it from the 3rd of May until the beginning of the aggression, that whole line and part of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Otherwise the matters in those two paragraphs are matters about which you learned from others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I saw with my very own eyes while I was passing by, because the evacuation route from Doboj of the population which we suggested, from the centre of town, that it should pass through Putnikovo hill and a Muslim settlement towards Tesanj, because all the other roads were completely blocked with the barricades that they had set up from all sides. They had surrounded Doboj from all sides, so you couldn't enter or exit Doboj at all except using that road. And we called it the road of evacuation towards the free territories up there, Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown his additional witness statement. That's Exhibit 562, tab 1. And if the witness could be shown the next exhibit, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, these are documents that were shown to you in The Hague, dated 13 October 1991. Can you tell us, please, what if anything you now about these decisions being passed in Serbian local communities at the time they were being passed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just summarise for us, please, what they are.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: These are decisions by Serb local communities of the Doboj municipality in which they proclaim the territory of the local community, that is to say that settlement, that the territory in actual fact will recognise only the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and some of the laws which are not in contravention to those laws of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And please turn to the first one of those decisions. It should be the decision relating -- of the local community of Majevac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Majevac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, which is the important article out of the articles we see on that first page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: The most important article is Article number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Well, what I said a moment ago. This is what it says in Article 2: "In the territory of this local community, positive federal laws and regulations will be implemented, as well as those regulations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which are not contrary to federal relations." And of course Article 1 in fact gives an overall explanation with respect to territory, which means the local community of Majevac in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, are they referring to the soon-to-be newly declared Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Not. That's the old name, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the composition of the federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The decisions which follow in the following pages, are they decisions of other local communities in the Doboj municipality relating to the same matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: In actual fact, it's all the same decision. The text is the same, the entire text, for each of the local communities, just the different community.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, these documents before you, again, decisions concerning Serbian local communities in Doboj, dated 13 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Please tell us briefly what those decisions relate to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: In these decisions, it is decided that the laws will be respected of the federal -- of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, just laws which are not in contravention to that. But these are being proclaimed on that particular territory and that particular local community.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, this document is dated the 16th of October, 1991. Please tell us briefly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Here the Serbian Democratic Party or, rather, the Municipal Board of the SDS of Doboj informs the Main Board of the SDS of Sarajevo that what we read before was implemented, the decisions, and we inform you that the Serb people of Doboj municipality reached the decision to proclaim the territories where they live an inseparable part of the federal state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which we herewith forward you. And then congratulations to Radovan Karadzic in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you know the -- Milan Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Is the signature at the bottom of the document in the B/C/S version that you have, is that his signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I can't say it's his because it says "for," for him. Now, the signature is similar, but I don't believe that this is his signature, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn, please, to tab 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please -- you can see it's self-evident on the face of that document what it is that that document is announcing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Here probably this is addressed because the signature is the president of the regional SDS board, which means for the nine municipalities of the Doboj municipality. This was probably sent to all the municipal boards, this announcement, saying that on such-and-such a day, a meeting would be held of all the municipal boards of Bosanska Krajina, the SDS Bosanska Krajina, and it also says here that Dr. Radovan Karadzic will be present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became aware of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I became aware that the meeting would take place, I think it was February 1992. I don't remember the exact date. But actually, I learnt about that several days prior to the meeting, in a closed meeting of the municipal boards of the SDS of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could you please turn to tab 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, this is an article from Derventski List newspaper, dated 13th of February, 1992. Were you shown this article and have you read it through in the premises -- in these premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I have read this article here, but I had this kind of article after a meeting that they held, because in that particular article, we have a description of the decisions reached at the meeting, who took the floor, who was criticised, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, to what meeting are you referring when you say that the article is referring to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: That meeting in February, the beginning of February. But I don't know the exact date. However, as this paper, the Derventski List is dated the 13th of February, that would make it five or six days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the first paragraph of that article. Does that first paragraph talk about the meeting to which you've been referring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The paragraph talks about a report by Milovan Bjelosevic. Is that one who was known to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: It's not Milovan Bjelosevic. It's Andrija Bjelosevic who was chief of the CSB of Doboj, because most probably the journalist here made a mistake and put Slobodan. However, in line three, it does say later on Andrija Milosevic -- Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In the 10th paragraph of the article, the name is in fact correctly stated as Andrija Bjelosevic. Witness, did you yourself know about the contents of that meeting at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Only after the meeting, after this paper had appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the next tab number, which is tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, can you take a look at that document and briefly describe what is being reported under the heading Doboj in that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: The municipal headquarters intelligence centre informs the republican intelligence centre about a bomb explosion that took place in the Proleterska Brigada Street in front of the Alf cafe. These are regular reports that were sent out towards the republic intelligence centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Is that an event about which you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I was present the next day, because I came to the spot to see what had happened. A bomb was thrown, had been thrown there. There were no casualties, but there was some material damage in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 9, please. We'll come back to tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, you've had an opportunity to read this document before today at the premises of the OTP. Can you tell us briefly what it is that the document is describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Actually, this is a document from the Ministry of Justice, the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which they inform the regions of Banja Luka, Sarajevo, (Sokolac, Trebinje Bijeljina and Doboj), about the organisation of jurisdiction and the judiciary on its territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Is it something that you knew about at the time, these activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I learnt about them later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you could turn, please, to the next document in the bundle. It's tab 10.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, did you listen to prior to seeing this document an intercepted conversation at the premises in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voices of the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Straight away. I recognise both right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us who the speakers were, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Here we have Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency of the day, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and she called up Andrije Bjelosevic, the chief of the CSB of Doboj, and she asked him to intervene with respect to a vehicle which in the Gracanica municipality the traffic police had been stopped and it was an ambulance which was full of medical sanitary corps material, which was on its way to the Croatian battlefront.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Probably around Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Pause there, please. Can you tell us, please, how you were able to recognise the voices of Biljana Plavsic and Andrije Bjelosevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, it's right, isn't it, that you cannot comment not knowing anything at the time about the matters as talked about in that intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: No. It was in another municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Next tab, please, tab 11. Witness, before seeing this transcript, did you listen to an intercepted -- a further intercepted conversation in these premises in The Hague, and did you identify the speakers during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Please tell us who those speakers were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the republican Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Radovan Karadzic, president of the SDS for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us briefly why it is or how it is that you were able to identify those speakers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I would hear both as a member of parliament attending Assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what if anything about the context of the conversation you're able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: The two of them are discussing and, actually, Krajisnik is asking Karadzic to convene an emergency meeting, and it probably refers to the meeting in Doboj with representatives of the SDS of Bosnian Krajina and leaders of the municipal boards that I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And just so -- for the benefit of the Chamber, if you could point out where in that transcript they're speaking about the meeting which you referred to a moment ago. Could you identify just how that relevant paragraph begins somewhere on the first page, I think a third of the way down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Here, under K, he says that they're having a meeting in Doboj at 12.00 tomorrow. It's actually Nikola Koljevic who had informed Krajisnik, and he's passing it on to Karadzic, that they're having a meeting of the three regions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: How are you able to conclude that that is a reference to the meeting about which you've referred earlier in your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: It is the meeting that was held in Doboj. The only one held in Doboj with representatives of these three regions of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I begin my cross-examination may I just make an observation? In view of the significance of the witness's position, which I cannot mention in open session but you're aware of it, both in the Party of Democratic Action and in the state bodies and a whole series of questions that have been addressed during the examination which you see yourself how long it lasted, I hope that you assume that my position is that this witness is not at all suitable as a 92 bis witness, because I -- so therefore, I should certainly have more time for the cross-examination than you regularly envisage according to the programme I'm given and the time I am given -- I am given for 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What I have also in mind is the fact that additional evidence was allowed under Rule 89(F). We will take that matter into account when we decide on the length of time that you should have. However, it starts on the basis that the witness was a 92 bis witness and, therefore, one hour. He was rather over half an hour in examination-in-chief, so I would think I speak entirely for myself that an hour and a half, something of that order, would be the right sort of time for you, but we will discuss that. Judge Kwon agrees. But any way, you'll get more than half an hour -- I mean more than one hour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1445, since you are -- you have a pseudonym and a protected witness, I won't mention your name or functions in Doboj and within the Party of Democratic Action in view of those positions, can you meritoriously address all the events that occurred in Doboj during the time period you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About the aggression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes. What aggression are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The aggression on Doboj. Very well. We'll come to that. Tell me, please, before the introduction of the multi-party system, as you put it, was life peaceful, inter-ethnic relations good? There was no tension or conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was your party, the SDA, that was the first party formed on an ethnic basis in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I think this question is irrelevant, because one party always has to be the first one to be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But yours was the first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the first, because there were many parties, but probably among the three, if you have in mind the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA, probably, yes. I don't know whether that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were the first to form a party on an ethnic basis, and you yourself say that until ethnic parties were formed, relations were good.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: The SDA was not a party formed on an ethnic basis. It was formed of all people who wished to join that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your opinion that the SDA is not a Muslim party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: The SDA had within its ranks even members of Serb ethnicity, and there are some even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It would be interesting to see how many. You're one of the founders of the SDA, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the prevalent opinion was that the SDA was to blame for the break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: That is your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was that the prevalent opinion in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that at first you wanted Yugoslavia to be preserved.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is it true also that the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina guaranteed equality of all constituent peoples, the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was regular practice that no important -- important decision of any -- of vital significance for any ethnic group could not be adopted without a consensus of all three?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes, but within the framework of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslim and Croat deputies in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 15th of October, 1991, took a decision on the sovereignty of that republic without Serb members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: They didn't decide on sovereignty. They just informed the European Union, asking them for international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: They couldn't make such a decision, because if they could, they certainly wouldn't have asked the European Union to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's easy to distinguish what is what, but is it true that in view of the fact that the decision was made without Serb representatives that it was in violent -- in flagrant violation of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that on the basis of the letter of the constitution or is it your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: On the basis of the rules of procedure of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the rules of procedure could not be in contravention of the constitution of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you disclaiming the fact that the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were one of the constituent peoples without whose will no consensus could be reached regarding a constitutional matter of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Deputies in the republican Assemblies from the SDS were not the only representatives of the Serb people. There were also deputies in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were Serbs and who belonged to other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that number of those was quite negligible. Isn't that right, Mr. 1445?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Just now I can't tell you how many there were, but in any event, the SDP and reformist parties had quite a number of Serb representatives in the BH parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The formation of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, I assume you will agree with me, was primarily the goal of the Muslim leadership and particularly of the SDA leader Izetbegovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: No. It was not only the goal of Bosniak representatives but also of Croats and all those who considered Bosnia and Herzegovina their own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You remember Izetbegovic's statement that he would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not in dispute, I assume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1445
